comment:
as a citizen who pays taxes, I am writing to urge EPA to extend Clean Water Act protections to Tribal nations.

Water quality standards are crucial to protecting environmental integrity and human health. Yet, today the United States is home to over 300 Tribes with reservations, but only 47 have EPA-approved water quality standards. That is why EPA must quickly act to extend the same Clean Water Act safeguards that currently exist in the rest of the United States to Tribal waters
This rule would establish water quality requirements for reservations, facilitate Tribal participation in managing water quality, provide a basis for enforcement, and protect reservation waters from upstream pollutant discharges. Establishing water quality standards that are protective of Tribal reserved rights and resources also supports healthier ecosystems, and ultimately, cleaner waters for everyone.

- Ensure that the standards are consistent with 40 CFR Part 131 and contain use designations consistent with the provisions of sections 101(a)(2) and 303(c)(2) of the CWA. This is not satisfied by simply adopting use designations to protect only 101(a)(2) uses.
- Establish Public Water Supply as a default designated use and numeric and narrative criteria adequate to protect that use in all covered waters, including but not limited to numeric limits on metals, pathogens, and organic chemicals and narrative prohibitions on taste and odor problems, the presence of oil and grease, and on waters being toxic, carcinogenic, mutagenic, or teratogenic to humans.
- Adopt numeric criteria for toxic pollutants consistent with Clean Water Act section 303(c)(2)(B) and the National Recommended Water Quality Criteria under Clean Water Act Section 304(a) to protect aquatic life and human health and supplement those criteria with narrative standards rather than only adopting limited narrative standards.
- Adopt numeric and narrative criteria to protect recreational uses consistent with EPA’s 2012 Recreational Water Quality Criteria (RWQC) for Bacterial Indicators of Fecal Contamination and 2019 Recreational Water Quality Criteria or Swimming Advisories for Cyanotoxins. The proposed narrative criteria do not expressly address or meaningfully protect recreational uses.
- Adopt numeric criteria for pathogens in coastal waters consistent with Clean Water Act section 303(i)(1)(A).
- Adopt numeric criteria for nutrients consistent with EPA’s Recommended Ambient Water Quality Criteria for Nutrients and supplement those criteria with narrative standards, such as prohibiting pollutants that lead to excessive growth of periphyton, phytoplankton, or aquatic macrophyte communities which impairs any existing or designated beneficial use.
- Adopt numeric and narrative biocriteria to protect aquatic life and supplement those criteria with narrative standards, including but not limited to criteria to protect fish consumption uses.
- Revise this proposed language, “All waters shall be free from toxic, radioactive, conventional, non-conventional, deleterious or other polluting substances in amounts that will prevent attainment of the applicable baseline designated uses,” as follows:
-- Ensure that the waters will be free of toxic pollution in toxic amounts without the added requirement that a baseline designated use be impaired. This is especially important given the fact that the agency is not proposing to protect public water supply as a baseline designated use, but even if that use is added, the prohibition should extend to all waters and impacts.
-- Ensure that criteria for discharges of radioactive pollution are at least as stringent as required under Clean Water Act Section 301(f) and are not limited to only the baseline designated uses.
- Eliminate provisions that allow the adoption of variances and designated use removal without additional rulemaking.

comment:
It is shocking to learn that 50 years after the Clean Water Act, or CWA (the Act) implementation there are still large swaths of unprotected surface waters. Over half a million people from over 250 Tribes will be affected by the proposed Federal Baseline Water Quality Standards for Indian Reservations rule: Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2016–0405 which is a major step toward creating a more equitable Union. I live and work in Oklahoma which is made up of many Indigenous people’s reservations of which this proposed rule will directly affect. It must be noted; however, that many Tribes lack funding to implement water quality standards (WQSs) which will require program development, implementation and enforcement resources, and educational funding. With over a quarter of US Indigenous peoples living in poverty, it is important to create a robust protection program for Waters of the US (WOTUS) without creating unnecessary financial burdens for Tribes. The US Government Accountability Office found that “many tribes have limited capacity to identify and access [assistance] programs and may not be aware of the federal assistance available” (GAO 2022). The EPA must support a funding mechanism that incorporates education to ensure CWA implementation.

comment: I'm writing in support of establishing baseline WQS for all Indian reservations. This proposed rule will help to alleviate further damage as a result of previous EPA decisions, for example, in the case of them excluding reservations from WQS approvals. As mentioned; the number of Tribes without TAS authority is still quite high, and the process of completing both the process of application and the development of applicable WQS could take more than a decade at the current pace. The creation of baseline WQS will help to protect Tribal lands from damage in the case of point source pollution, which is a problem in these areas that lack applicable WQS, and leaves water sources inadequately protected from pollution. By bringing these areas under protection of the CWA, it will offer some protection against pollution, and recourse against polluters, until Tribes obtain TAS and are able to develop WQS in accordance with their own environmental goals and those of the CWA. However, any rule ought to offer both general protection and alternatives to the current process of obtaining WQS, should a Tribe opt to avoid seeking TAS for any number of reasons.

comment:
I am commenting on the proposed regulation as a concerned citizen who has traveled extensively throughout the United States and seen how different water quality standards, or no water quality standards, have been applied to the reservations. I fully support the independence of the Indian and Alaska Native Tribes, but also see that having reasonable water quality standards as proposed by the EPA and agreed to by the governing bodies of the Tribes, would be of great benefit to the members of the Tribes.
The goals of applying the Clean Water Act to Indian Reservations seem simple enough, provide better quality water for the residents of the reservations. Maintaining or improving the water quality to support aquatic life and to benefit the health of people who consume the aquatic life seems like common sense. The goal of maintaining or improving the water quality to enhance recreational activities in and on the water also makes perfect sense. Adding the requirement to protect cultural and traditional uses of waterways shows that the EPA has been listening to the Tribes and has incorporated their feedback into the proposed regulation.
The EPA appears to have been conscientious in seeking input from the Tribes and has not rushed the process. With the end of the comment period approaching quickly I would hope that a regulation satisfactory to the Tribes is approved, and meaningful water quality standard can be implemented for a long-overlooked section of the population.
